findings.problem: Line 4 frames the jealousy as a reaction to the message ("Same message, two reactions... some are filled with jealousy and contradict it"). Acts 13:45 gives a different reason: the Jews were filled with jealousy when they "saw the crowds" that had gathered on the following Sabbath (Acts 13:44-45). Their contradicting is aimed at what Paul was saying, but the jealousy is about the crowds. The line should keep the text's own reason, for example: "When they see the crowds, some are filled with jealousy and contradict what Paul is saying."

rule.text: Papa Dorin can retell in his own words and fill in what the text clearly implies. Scene-setting details are fine. He never says anything the text shows is wrong.

findings.problem: Line 5 says "the Lord had already said" before the quotation. Acts 13:47 calls it a command: "For this is what the Lord has commanded us." The prep card for this verse (stop 3, card 9) keeps "commanded." The Big Idea should too, for example: "because this is what the Lord commanded them: ..."

rule.text: Call things what the text calls them.

findings.problem: Line 6 brings in Luke ("And how does Luke close out the chapter?"). This is the first and only time he appears in the lesson, and he isn't introduced. Luke isn't named anywhere in Acts 13:13-52, and no prep card mentions him.

rule.text: New people. The first time someone shows up, he says simply who they are, like "Cyrus, king of Persia" or "Moses, Israel's leader."

findings.problem: Line 6 says Luke is the author of Acts. That comes from church tradition, not from the passage, and it has no reference. The docs say "Every Bible fact he states carries its reference," but they don't say whether Papa Dorin can name a book's traditional author when Scripture doesn't name them.
findings.question: Can Papa Dorin name a book's traditional author (here Luke for Acts) when the BSB text doesn't name them? If he can, how should he introduce them, and what reference does the claim need? If he can't, should he say "the passage" or "the chapter" instead?

findings.problem: The Big Idea has 7 entries, which meets "about 5 to 7 lines." But most entries run 2 to 4 sentences (for example, line 3 has four sentences and line 5 has three plus a long quote), so the whole thing is around 400 words. big-idea.md says "Each line is one entry" but doesn't say how long one entry can be. A long entry can stretch the "5 to 7 lines" limit well past what it seems to allow.
findings.question: Does "about 5 to 7 lines" also limit how long each line is, such as one or two sentences, or a word count? Or can a single entry hold several sentences?
